title: Northbridge: restoring the floodplain
text:
This is an invented teaching example, not a real municipal study. Northbridge's planning group compared two flood responses: restoring an upstream wetland and raising the wall around the town centre. Their scenario describes a wall that protects the centre but pushes water downstream. A restored wetland temporarily stores part of the floodwater and releases it more slowly.

The group recommends considering wetland restoration before further wall construction because the wetland changes the catchment's storage rather than moving the peak elsewhere. This preference is conditional. Available land, soil contamination, flood magnitude and maintenance capacity can change the decision. The handbook does not claim that wetlands prevent every flood.

The wall may still be needed around critical infrastructure. The proposed sequence is to assess the catchment, restore suitable storage, then size remaining hard defences for residual risk. The argument combines local protection with downstream responsibility.
summary: In an invented Northbridge planning scenario, wetland restoration is considered before taller walls because it adds temporary catchment storage instead of transferring peak flow downstream. This is a conditional recommendation, dependent on land, contamination, flood magnitude and maintenance. Walls can remain necessary for critical infrastructure and residual risk. The unit argues for a catchment-wide sequence rather than a universal ban on hard defences.

title: Flood risk across municipal boundaries
text:
This fictional lecture examines the ethical boundary of a flood project. A wall that reduces flood exposure inside one district can increase the peak in another. A project should therefore be evaluated over the connected catchment rather than only inside the paying district.

The lecturer distinguishes reducing total harm from reallocating it. In the Northbridge example, upstream storage is attractive because slowing the flood can help multiple settlements. That does not show that every upstream project is fair. A landowner who loses productive land deserves consideration, and affected communities need a voice.

The lecture concludes that downstream effects, distribution of costs and participation should be explicit parts of the decision. Hydrological performance alone cannot settle the political question of who bears the burden.
summary: This fictional lecture argues that flood projects should be assessed across connected districts. A protective wall may relocate harm, while storage can reduce peak flow for several communities. Storage still creates local burdens, so compensation and participation matter. Engineering performance and distributive fairness are related but distinct questions.

title: Maintenance changes the comparison
text:
The Northbridge teaching case assumes both wetlands and walls require ongoing care. A wetland can lose capacity through sediment accumulation, blocked outlets or changed land use. A wall can deteriorate through neglected gates, damaged foundations or increasing water pressure. Neither option is maintenance-free.

The group therefore compares projects over their service lives. A small capital budget does not justify selecting a project whose operating costs cannot be met. Conversely, a larger upfront restoration cost may be reasonable if it improves storage and habitat while remaining maintainable.

These are scenario assumptions for discussing decisions, not measured cost estimates. A real project would require local inspection, engineering evidence and a funded maintenance plan.
summary: This fictional handbook chapter makes maintenance part of the wetlands-versus-walls comparison. Wetlands and hard defences can both lose effectiveness without care. Decisions should consider service-life budgets and multiple benefits, without inventing numerical cost claims. Real projects require local evidence and funded maintenance.

title: Planning for uncertainty
text:
A fictional planning workshop asks what happens when future rainfall exceeds the design scenario. Participants reject a promise of complete safety. They instead compare several plausible floods and identify how each project fails.

Wetland storage has finite capacity. Once full, further rainfall must still travel downstream. Walls also have finite design limits and can be overtopped. Combining storage, targeted defences, warnings and evacuation routes can address different parts of the risk.

The purpose of the exercise is to replace a single best-case forecast with explicit assumptions and adaptation options. It does not establish numerical probabilities for future rainfall.
summary: This invented workshop note emphasizes finite capacities and failure modes. Wetlands can fill and walls can be overtopped. A combined strategy may address different risks. It calls for scenario comparisons and adaptation rather than promises of complete protection or unsupported numerical probabilities.

title: Habitat benefits and flood decisions
text:
In this invented podcast discussion, two planners consider the additional habitat benefits of a wetland. They agree that these benefits can matter in a public decision. They disagree about whether habitat value should compensate for a project that performs poorly on flood risk.

One speaker argues for a minimum flood-performance requirement followed by a comparison of wider benefits. The other warns that a narrow performance rule can ignore long-term ecological damage caused by hard defences.

The transcript offers contrasting decision principles. It does not report a real interview, species count, monetary valuation or field experiment.
summary: This fictional podcast contrasts two ways of combining habitat value and flood performance: a minimum safety threshold followed by wider-benefit comparison, versus a broader ecological assessment. It records a disagreement rather than an empirical result or a resolved recommendation.

title: Protecting a hospital
text:
The Northbridge scenario includes a hospital whose services must continue during a flood. Restoring upstream wetlands may reduce exposure but cannot guarantee access or power. The planning group therefore considers a targeted barrier, protected electrical equipment and alternative access routes.

The example illustrates why considering wetlands first does not imply rejecting all walls. Different interventions address different failure modes. The hospital plan depends on the remaining risk after catchment measures have been assessed.

No actual hospital is described. The unit is an invented example of layered risk management, not an engineering specification.
summary: This invented hospital case shows why catchment restoration and targeted hard defences can complement each other. Wetlands may reduce exposure without guaranteeing power or access. The unit supports layered measures for residual risk and explicitly rejects interpreting the restoration-first proposal as a ban on walls.

title: Keeping an auditable decision record
text:
The Northbridge methods note asks planners to keep each original proposal, the assumptions used in comparison and the reasons for later revisions. A short summary can help locate a proposal but should not replace the full argument when a decision is contested.

The fictional group links each recommendation to a dated source unit and keeps quotations separate from interpretation. The final decision packet contains a complete leading proposal, summaries of alternatives and specific passages about disputed details.

This is an illustration of evidence organization. It is not a claim that a particular software system has improved real municipal decisions.
summary: This fictional methods note distinguishes finding a source through its summary from evaluating its complete argument. It recommends preserving original proposals, assumptions and revisions, and building a decision packet from a full leading proposal, alternative summaries and disputed passages.
